title: Cloud Key Management
summary: Cloud key management is the practice of creating, storing, using, rotating and retiring cryptographic keys through a provider's managed service rather than inside application code. The service holds key material in hardware security modules, so keys can be used for encrypt and decrypt operations without the raw bytes ever being exportable. Most designs rely on envelope encryption: a data key encrypts the payload, and a longer-lived key encryption key wraps that data key, which avoids re-encrypting large volumes of data whenever the top-level key rotates. A key policy or identity policy separately controls who may use a key, so authorisation and cryptography remain two distinct decisions. It appears wherever data is protected at rest, across object storage, managed databases, disk volumes, message queues and secret stores. The common mistake is believing the managed service removes customer responsibility. Teams still hard-code key material into pipelines, reuse one key across unrelated systems, and disable deletion protection, so a single misconfigured lifecycle rule or a stolen deployment credential undoes the whole control.

beginner.definition: Cryptographic keys are the secret strings of characters that lock and unlock your data. Cloud key management means using a service from your cloud provider to create, store, and change those keys safely. The keys stay inside protected hardware, so your team never copies them into code. You control who may use a key.
beginner.whyItMatters: If a key leaks, an attacker can read or change everything that key protects. Keys that never change give an attacker unlimited time to use a stolen copy. Copying keys into program code spreads them to laptops, build servers, and chat messages. A managed key service keeps the key material in one guarded place and records every use. It also lets you retire a key quickly when someone leaves the team.
howItWorks: Create a key inside the provider's protected hardware, so the secret never appears on a normal computer disk.
Give each key one clear job, and keep that job small. Let it protect one database or one set of backups, and do not share it everywhere.
Encrypt data with a short lived data key. Then wrap that data key with a longer lived key held by the service.
Record every use of the key in an audit log, so you can see who decrypted what and when.
Rotate keys on a schedule and after any suspicion, which limits how long a stolen copy stays useful.
Delete or disable keys carefully, with a waiting period and a second approval, because lost keys mean lost data.
beginner.example: Think of a school caretaker who keeps every door key in a locked cabinet in the office. Teachers do not carry master keys home. When a teacher needs the sports hall, the caretaker opens that one door and writes the time in a book. If a key is lost, the caretaker changes that one lock and notes it. Cloud key management is that cabinet. The provider guards the cabinet. Your rules say who may ask for which door, and the log book shows every opening. Nobody copies the keys, so nobody can quietly come back later.
takeaways: Keep key material inside a managed key service, never in code, chat messages, or shared configuration files.
Use a separate key for each important system, so one leak does not open everything you own.
Plan rotation and a waiting period before deletion, because a deleted key cannot be brought back.

objectives: Explain what a cryptographic key is and why cloud providers offer managed key storage.
Describe envelope encryption and the different roles of data keys and key encryption keys.
Identify the controls that surround a cloud key, such as rotation, access policy and audit logging.
Recognise risky practices such as hard coded keys and a single shared key for all systems.
Explain how key deletion and separation of duties affect recovery.
